## Today's Agenda

- Three rounds of peer review
- Turn the two reviews you receive into a revision list
- Draft the reflection paragraph
- Deploy your site before you leave, with the [Chapter 14 starter file](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/14-publishing-your-paper.qmd)

## Today Is a Working Session

[Last class of the term]{.eyebrow}

- There is no lecture: three rounds of review, then your revision list
    - You read two papers, and two people read yours
- Then you draft the reflection in class, while the study is fresh
- Help with rendering and deployment is in the room the whole session

Leave today knowing exactly what is left to do.

## What You Should Have in Hand

- A rendered draft, even if some sections are thin
    - Thin is expected. A rough draft is the point of today
- Your three figures, produced by code inside the document
- Your test output: the means, the statistic, *p*, and the effect size
- A project that builds without error

If your render is broken, say so now.

## The White Paper, 250 Points

- The largest piece of the course, due Friday, December 18, 11:59 PM
- Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, and References
    - Plus your one-paragraph Reflection
- You submit two things, both required: the PDF (in the docs folder inside your White Paper folder, after a render) and the live URL of your GitHub Pages site
- It is graded on the study, the writing, and whether it reproduces from the code

## Where the 250 Points Sit

- **Introduction:** 30
- **Methods:** 60
- **Results:** 50
- **Discussion:** 50
- **Abstract and references:** 20
- **Reproducibility and publication:** 25
- **Reflection:** 15

## Reading the Rubric

The full rubric is in the [White Paper entry](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/mc451-assignments.html#white-paper) on the Assignments page. Read it as five questions:

- Does the paper answer its own question?
- Could someone else repeat the study from the Methods?
- Are the numbers complete: means, test, *p*, and effect size?
- Is the paper honest about its limits?
- Does the site deploy?

## Exercise: State Your Claim in One Sentence {.discuss}

- State the one sentence your paper is actually claiming
- Restate it without the words "significant" or "*p*-value"
- If it takes you more than one sentence, name the part you are unsure of

## Round One, the Introduction

Read your partner's Introduction only. Answer each question in writing:

- After the first paragraph, do you know what the question is?
- Is the theory doing work in the argument, or is it decoration?
- Does the Introduction promise only what the study can deliver?
- Name one sentence that could be cut with no loss

## Round Two, the Methods

Read the Methods only. Answer each question in writing:

- Could you repeat this study? Name the first place you would stall
- Is the sample described: how many cases, drawn how, from what population?
- Is each coding rule clear enough that you would code the same way?
- Are the choices disclosed: bins, caps, filters, and dropped cases?

## Round Three, the Results and Discussion

Read the Results and Discussion. Answer each question in writing:

- Does every figure have a label, units, and a sentence saying what it shows?
- Is the test reported in full, with the effect size?
- Does the Discussion claim more than the Results support?
- Are the stated limits real limits, or apologies?

## What a Useful Review Sounds Like

- **Not useful:** "This is good, maybe add more detail"
- **Useful:** "I could not tell whether your cases were drawn at random. Say which, in paragraph two"
- Point at a location, name the problem, and suggest one fix
- You are not grading. You are the first reader who is not the author

## Common Problems Reviewers Find

- The Introduction and the Results answer different questions
- The effect size is missing, so "significant" claims more than it should
- Default axis labels, still reading `message_length`
- A cap or filter that is in the code and never mentioned in the prose
- The Discussion says "proves." Nothing in a study like this proves anything

## Back at Your Own Paper

Turn the two reviews you received into one list with three parts:

- **Must fix:** anything that makes the paper wrong or unreadable
- **Should fix:** clarity, labels, and tighter prose
- **Disagree, and here is why:** you are the author, and you may decline a suggestion with a reason

Then save the list:

- Save it in your White Paper folder: **File**, then **New Text File**, type the list, then **File**, **Save As**, and name it revision-list.txt
- It is your plan for finals week

## The Reflection Paragraph

- One paragraph. It is not part of IMRaD and it is not a result
- It is your candid account of what the study taught you
    - What turned out harder than expected
    - Where a coding rule proved ambiguous in practice
    - What the dataset could not answer, and why
    - What a second attempt would change

## What a Good Reflection Avoids

- **The bland version:** "Everything went well and I learned a lot"
- **The anxious version:** "Everything went wrong and I am sorry"
- A reflection is evidence of judgment, not an apology
- Saying precisely where a study is weak is proof that you understand it

One honest paragraph beats a page of hedging.

## Render and Deploy Before You Leave

- Commit and push first: Source Control, a message, Commit, then Sync Changes ([Commit and Push with Git](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc451/12-commit-and-push-with-git.html))

```r
v2v::deploy_portfolio(project)
```

- `project` is your White Paper folder's name, set in Step 2 of the [Chapter 14 starter file](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/starters/14-publishing-your-paper.qmd)
- When it asks `Publish to GitHub Pages? [y/N]`, click in the R terminal, type `y`, and press **Enter**
- A failed check names the one thing to fix ([Publish Your Site](https://aura-lab.siue.edu/v2v-hub/guides/mc451/13-publish-your-site.html))
- Run it today, even on an unfinished draft: a deployment failure is much easier to fix with help in the room

## Checkpoint

Before you leave today you should have:

- Two written reviews, handed to their authors
- Two reviews of your own paper, in hand
- A three-part revision list saved in your project
- A first draft of your reflection paragraph
- A successful deploy, or a specific error message and a plan to fix it
